questions.q: What thresholds does Theo's k6 load test check checkout-api against?
options: Total dollar cost of the test run
p95 latency under 300ms and an error rate under 1%
Number of availability zones used
Exact replica count at all times
questions.explain: The k6 test defines real SLO thresholds — http_req_duration p(95)<300 and http_req_failed rate<0.01 — and both pass comfortably in the results.

questions.q: Where does the load test's synthetic traffic originate from?
options: Thousands of real shopper devices across the country
500 virtual users, all generated from a single Azure DevOps pipeline agent in one region
A distributed botnet of test clients across multiple clouds
Traffic replayed directly from last year's sale
questions.explain: k6's virtual users all originate from one pipeline agent in one Azure region — a standard, reasonable single-origin synthetic test setup.

questions.q: What does this load test's results actually prove?
options: Nothing — the test is meaningless
That checkout-api meets its latency and error-rate SLOs under roughly 500 concurrent virtual users' worth of volume, with the HPA scaling cleanly from 6 to 18 replicas
That pods are evenly distributed across all three availability zones
That the FinOps dashboard is broken
questions.explain: The test answers exactly the question it was built to answer — SLO compliance under volume — and answers it cleanly; that's a real, valid result, not a false pass.

questions.q: What specific traffic pattern does this test NOT reproduce, and why does that matter?
options: High latency requests, which the test can't generate

A rapid, bursty, multi-origin scale-out — the exact condition under which the scheduler is most likely to concentrate new pods onto whichever nodes/zones have room at that moment, absent a topology spread constraint
HTTPS traffic, since the test only uses HTTP
Requests to checkout-api specifically, since it only tests catalog-api
questions.explain: A smooth, single-origin ramp gives the scheduler time to place pods evenly; it never creates the sudden, uneven scheduling pressure a bursty real sale will, which is exactly when the missing topologySpreadConstraints from Lesson 4 would matter.

questions.q: How does the lesson characterize the fact that this gap wasn't caught by the load test?
options: As a careless mistake by Theo that should have been caught
As a gap in what load testing was scoped to mean going into the sale, not a process failure — nobody had identified AZ-skew under bursty scale-out as a distinct risk to test for separately
As proof the load test was poorly designed from the start
As irrelevant, since the sale will go smoothly regardless
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the test was reasonable and the result was a real pass — the second question (AZ distribution under bursty scale-out) simply wasn't identified as something to test for separately.
